newsitem.title: USA: U.S. condemns "terrorist attack" on Syrian bus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. condemns "terrorist attack" on Syrian bus.

text.p: The United States, responding to Syrian complaints, on Friday condemned a bus bombing in Damascus as a "terrorist attack" and offered condolences to the victims' families.
But the State Department continued to criticise Syria for accusing Israel of complicity in Tuesday's bombing, which killed nine people and wounded 44.

"The United States condemns this terrorist attack against innocent people. And there is every reason to believe that these were innocent people on that bus -- civilians who ought not have to fear for their lives when they travel around the city of Damascus," department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"And the United States extends our condolences to the families of the victims. The United States would have made this statement yesterday, had we known about the incident in any kind of detail," he said.

But on Syria's continued charges that Israel was responsible for the attack, Burns said: "It is not wise for any government to accuse another government of an act of terrorism without a foundation of evidence to support it."
"The United States is not aware of any evidence whatsoever that would link the Israeli government ... to the bomb attack of a couple of days ago ... or the other bombings in Damascus," he said.
He also stressed the Israeli government had condemned the bombing and denied any involvement.
Syria earlier rejected a U.S. warning on Thursday against blaming Israel and said the previous U.S. statement lacked sympathy for the families of the victims and disregarded Syrians' feelings.

Burns said on Thursday the United States could not confirm a Syrian report that Israeli agents planted the bus bomb and warned Damascus against making "wild and irresponsible" statements without evidence.
In that initial reaction, he did not condemn the attack -- as Washington routinely does in cases it considers terrorism -- or express sympathy for the victims' families.

On Friday, Burns explained his initial remarks were based only on news reports. "We didn't know exactly what had happened. We didn't know if anyone had been killed or if anyone had been wounded ... We had no independent information from the government of Syria," he said.
Subsequently, however, U.S. and Syrian officials had been in contact, including a call on Friday between Burns and the Syrian ambassador to Washington.

Burns refused to speculate on Syria's motives for laying blame for the attack on Israel. But the fault-finding is worrying to the Clinton administration which laboured hard over the past four years to negotiate peace between Israel and its main remaining Arab enemy, Syria.

Israeli-Syrian talks broke down months ago when the Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu became Israel's prime minister and U.S. officials say there are no signs negotiations could resume any time soon.
